---
title: "Squeeze Harder, Say \"Same\": Physical Effort Shifts Older Adults' Perceptual Criterion Without Reducing Sensitivity"
abstract: |
  Physical effort often accompanies perception in daily life, and its cost may grow with age. Sixty-eight older adults judged whether two tones or two visual gratings were the same or different while holding a light or a strong handgrip, with pupil diameter recorded throughout. Under the strong grip, participants reported a difference less often at every stimulus level, including when the two stimuli were identical, and their discrimination did not become less precise. Effort therefore shifted the criterion for reporting a difference toward "same" rather than degrading sensitivity, in line with earlier analyses of the same cohort. Pupil diameter during the grip did not differ reliably between grip levels, and the pupil response after the probe was smaller under the strong grip, a difference that overlaps with the release of the grip. Pupil size just before the probe was only weakly associated with how precisely participants discriminated on a given trial, and the pupil response after the probe was not associated with it at all. In older adults, physical effort appears to change how readily a difference is reported rather than how well it is perceived, and the pupil-linked arousal measured here did not account for that change.

# Introduction

Everyday perception often has to be done while the body is working, such as judging whether a sound has changed while holding a load. Combining a motor demand with a perceptual or cognitive one costs more with age. Older adults show larger dual-task costs than younger adults [@verhaeghen2003], and holding an effortful isometric grip lowered older adults' visual working-memory accuracy when distractors were present [@azer2023]. What such a demand does to a perceptual judgment is less clear.

A same–different judgment can change in two ways. If the sensory evidence becomes noisier, the psychometric function that relates the size of a difference to the probability of reporting it becomes shallower, and sensitivity falls. If the observer instead requires more evidence before reporting a difference, the function shifts toward larger differences without becoming shallower, and reports of a difference on trials with no difference become rarer as well [@macmillan2005detection; @prins2016psychophysics]. The two accounts mean different things for aging. A loss of sensitivity would mean that effort degrades what older adults perceive. A criterion shift would mean that effort changes how readily they report it.

Physical effort may act on the judgment through arousal. Isometric handgrip engages the locus coeruleus–noradrenergic (LC–NE) system, the main source of cortical noradrenaline and a regulator of arousal and attention [@mather2020isometric; @mather2016]. The locus coeruleus is among the brain structures most vulnerable to aging [@mather2016], which makes its role in effort-related changes in older adults' perception a natural question.

Pupil diameter offers a noninvasive index of this system. Pupil size covaries with locus coeruleus activity [@joshi2016], and adaptive gain theory distinguishes two signals [@astonjones2005]. Baseline pupil size tracks a slowly varying control state: larger baselines accompany disengagement from the task [@gilzenrat2010], and performance is best at intermediate baselines [@murphy2011]. The task-evoked pupil response tracks engagement with a particular stimulus or decision [@beatty1982; @gilzenrat2010]. If arousal links effort to the judgment, pupil size just before the stimulus to be judged is the most direct test, because it precedes the judgment it is meant to predict. The task-evoked response follows the stimulus and partly reflects the decision itself, so its association with the judgment is harder to interpret.

Three earlier analyses frame this chapter. In younger adults, Chapter 1 found that high effort enlarged the pupil in all tasks and impaired visual discrimination, with no interaction between effort and task difficulty [CONFIRM: Chapter 1 pupil result after the Chapter 1 time-axis check]. In the older adults studied here, per-participant psychometric functions showed that high grip raised thresholds without changing slopes, a pattern read as a more conservative criterion for "different" [@sun2026handgrip]. Chapter 3 fitted drift diffusion models to the same trials and found that high effort shifted the drift criterion toward "same" without reducing evidence quality. Whether pupil-linked arousal carries these effects from trial to trial has not been tested, and @sun2026handgrip name it as the next step.

This chapter asks two questions. The first is whether a high grip changes the criterion for reporting a difference, the sensitivity of the judgment, or both. A criterion account predicts fewer "different" responses at every stimulus difference, including when the two stimuli are identical, with no change in the slope of the psychometric function. A sensitivity account predicts a shallower slope under high effort. The second question is whether pupil size tracks the slope from trial to trial. Adaptive gain theory predicts that moments of higher tonic arousal, indexed by a larger pupil before the probe, accompany less precise discrimination. The task-evoked response was examined as a secondary predictor, and pupil size during the grip served as a physiological check that the grip raised arousal. All analyses were specified before they were run; the study was not pre-registered.

# Methods

## Participants and trials {#sec-participants}

Recruitment, exclusions, and demographics are those of @sun2026handgrip. The behavioral analysis uses that paper's cleaned trial file: `r v_int("m1_nobs")` trials from `r v_int("m1_n_participants")` participants (`r v_int("m1_n_adt")` auditory, `r v_int("m1_n_vdt")` visual). `r v_int("n_one_task")` participants completed only one task.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Age, sex, and education for the behavioral sample, by task, and for the participants in the task-evoked pupil sample. Education n counts participants with a numeric year value. Cells coded as less than 12 years, and blank cells, are not in the education mean. T-MoCA is not in the demographics file or the subject-by-task file supplied with the preprint share, so it is not in this table."

demo_tab <- read_export("tbl_demographics.csv")
stopifnot(nrow(demo_tab) == 4L)
knitr::kable(demo_tab)
```

Pupil analyses use a subset of the same trials. A trial entered the pupil file only when a recording existed and the sample count and within-trial time step met the checks under Pupil measures (@sec-pupillometry). The grip-window model uses `r v_int("m2_nobs")` trials (`r v_int("m2_n_participants")` participants). The task-evoked models use `r v_int("m3_nobs")` trials (`r v_int("m3_n_participants")` participants; `r v_int("m3_n_adt")` auditory, `r v_int("m3_n_vdt")` visual). The missingness model uses the `r v_int("m5_nobs")` trials that could be matched to a pupil recording (`r v_int("m5_n_participants")` participants), of which `r v_int("m3_nobs")` passed the task-evoked gate. `r v_int("n_no_tepr")` of the `r v_int("m1_n_participants")` participants contributed no trials to the task-evoked models, because no recording existed or fewer than 20 trials passed the checks (@tbl-pupil-flow).

## Task {#sec-task-paradigm}

Participants completed an auditory and a visual same–different task in the scanner, one task per session, order counterbalanced. On each trial they held a left-hand grip at 5% or 40% of maximum voluntary contraction, saw or heard a standard and then a probe, judged whether the two were the same or different, and rated confidence. The inter-trial interval was 1.5–4.5 s [@sun2026handgrip]. @fig-paradigm shows the fixed sequence after squeeze onset. From squeeze onset, the standard began at 3.75 s and the probe at 4.35 s. At probe offset (4.45 s), a change in border color from salmon to light blue cued participants to release the grip. The same–different response window ran from 4.70 to 7.70 s, and the confidence window followed.

```{r}
#| label: fig-paradigm
#| fig-cap: "Trial sequence for the auditory and visual same–different tasks. The inter-trial interval is 1.5–4.5 s. Times after squeeze onset follow the schematic. Low effort is 5% and high effort is 40% of maximum voluntary contraction (MVC)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| out-width: "75%"
#| fig-align: center

paradigm_path <- file.path(proj_root, "07_manuscript", "chapter2", "output", "figures", "Paradigm.png")
stopifnot(file.exists(paradigm_path))
knitr::include_graphics(paradigm_path)
```

Auditory probes were 1,000 Hz or 1,000 Hz plus 8, 16, 32, or 64 Hz. Visual probes matched a standard Gabor or raised its contrast by 0.06, 0.12, 0.24, or 0.48. The zero-offset trials are catch trials: the standard and the probe were the same.

Stimuli were presented with Psychtoolbox 3.0.18 in MATLAB R2022b [@brainard1997] on a PROPixx projector (480 Hz, 1920 × 1080) viewed through a head-coil mirror at 12 cm. Auditory stimuli used MRI-safe earbuds. Grip force was recorded with a Current Designs dynamometer at 100 Hz. The eye tracker was a binocular TRACKPixx sampling at 2,000 Hz. Pupil diameter was recorded in arbitrary units and analyzed at 250 Hz, after blinks and other artifacts were removed with ET-Remove-Artifacts [@mather2020isometric]. Maximum voluntary contraction was the mean of three squeezes, measured in Session 1 and again in the scanner.

## Pupil measures {#sec-pupillometry}

Each trial was epoched from 3 s before squeeze onset at 250 Hz, so sample $k$ falls at $t_k = -3 + 0.004(k - 1)$ s. A trial was retained when it had 3,425 or 3,426 samples and its median time step was within $10^{-6}$ of 0.004 s.

Four summaries were taken from that axis. The pre-squeeze baseline is the mean over $[−0.5, 0)$ s. Pre-probe pupil is the mean diameter over $[3.85, 4.35)$ s, ending at probe onset; because the window follows the standard (3.75–3.85 s), it contains the early response to the standard. The grip-window mean is the mean over $[1.0, 4.35]$ s, corrected by the pre-squeeze baseline. The task-evoked pupillary response (TEPR) is the mean dilation over $[4.65, 7.65]$ s after subtracting the pre-probe pupil. Each summary required at least half of its own samples to be finite. A participant entered a pupil model only with at least 20 such trials in that task.

The TEPR window begins after probe offset, so grip release, the release cue, the response screen, and the button press all fall inside it. Of the pupil measures, only the pre-probe measure precedes the probe.

The primary TEPR summary is the mean, not the area under the curve. On these trials the area tracks the mean times the proportion of finite samples. The area is reported only in the supplement.

State and trait were computed inside each model's sample. State is the trial value minus the mean of that participant and task, divided by the pooled within-cell standard deviation. Trait is the participant-by-task mean on that same scale. Within a participant and task, the state mean is zero by construction.

## Coding and models {#sec-models}

The behavioral outcome is the binary "different" response. Catch is an indicator for the zero-offset trial. On the four nonzero offsets, the offset index is 0, 1, 2, or 3 and the centered offset is that index minus 1.5, so the values are −1.5, −0.5, 0.5, and 1.5. On catch trials the centered offset is set to 0. Effort is sum-coded, high = +0.5 and low = −0.5. Task is sum-coded, visual = +0.5 and auditory = −0.5. A coefficient on effort is the high-minus-low difference on the model's link scale.

Five models were fit with lme4 `r v("lme4_version")` and lmerTest `r v("lmerTest_version")` [@bates2015; @kuznetsova2017lmerTest], using bobyqa with a maximum of 200,000 function evaluations. A fit was accepted only when it was not singular and the optimizer returned no convergence message. If a maximal model [@barr2013] failed that rule, the random-effects structure was reduced in fixed steps: correlated slopes, then uncorrelated slopes, then removal of the random slope with the smallest variance, then a random intercept only [@bates2015]. Each step is listed in the Supplement. Wald 95% intervals are reported. For the linear models the degrees of freedom are Satterthwaite approximations. No equivalence bound was set, and no correction was applied across models. Each model answers a different question. A null result is the estimate and its interval.

**Behavior (M1).** All `r v_int("m1_nobs")` trials. Probit regression of "different" on catch, centered offset, effort, and task, with all interactions, and a by-participant random slope for each of those four terms. The criterion terms are the effort coefficient and its interaction with catch. The sensitivity term is the offset-by-effort interaction.

**Grip-window pupil (M2).** Linear model of the grip-window mean on effort and task, with a by-participant random slope for effort. This is a physiological check on whether the grip changed pupil diameter during the hold. The published manipulation check is grip force, not pupil [@sun2026handgrip].

**Task-evoked pupil (M3).** Linear model of the TEPR mean on effort, task, catch, and centered offset, with by-participant random slopes for effort and offset.

**Pupil and sensitivity (M4).** Probit models on the same `r v_int("m4a_nobs")` trials as M3. The primary predictor is pre-probe pupil (M4a). The secondary predictor is the TEPR mean (M4b). Both include state and trait, and both keep effort and task so the pupil coefficients are estimated within effort and task. The sensitivity term is the offset-by-state interaction.

**Missing pupil data (M5).** Logistic model of whether a matched trial passed the TEPR gate, with effort, task, catch, centered offset, and a by-participant intercept.

Models were estimated in R [@R]. The chapter was rendered with Quarto [@quarto].

# Results

## High effort lowered "different" responses at every offset {#sec-behavior}

@fig-p-diff shows the proportion of "different" responses at each offset. Pooling trials, the proportion was lower under high effort at every offset in both tasks. Averaged over participants, as plotted, it was lower at every offset except the 0.24 contrast offset in the visual task. Responding was near ceiling at the largest offset, with proportions of `r v("top_adt_p")` in the auditory task and `r v("top_vdt_p")` in the visual task, and there the high-minus-low difference in proportion was `r v("level4_adt_diff_prop")` (auditory) and `r v("level4_vdt_diff_prop")` (visual). On catch trials, the proportion of "different" responses was `r v("catch_adt_p")` in the auditory task and `r v("catch_vdt_p")` in the visual task.

# Discussion

Older adults holding a strong grip reported a difference less often at every stimulus difference, in both modalities, including on catch trials, on which the two stimuli were identical. The additional change on catch trials was close to zero, so false alarms fell along with responses at the other offsets, and the slope of the psychometric function did not become shallower. This is the pattern a shift of the criterion toward "same" predicts, not the pattern a loss of sensitivity predicts [@macmillan2005detection]. Three analyses of these participants now agree. Per-participant psychometric functions showed higher thresholds and unchanged slopes [@sun2026handgrip], the trial-level model reported here showed the criterion pattern directly, and the diffusion models of Chapter 3 placed the effect in the drift criterion rather than in evidence quality. The trial-level model also addresses a limitation of the per-participant fits: with 75 trials per grip level, individual slopes are estimated imprecisely [@sun2026handgrip], whereas a model that pools all trials estimates the change in slope across participants, and it still showed no shallowing. The offset-by-effort interaction was positive, but the effort difference was smallest at the largest offset, where responding was near ceiling, and a probit model without a lapse rate can express a difference that shrinks near ceiling as a steeper slope. The positive term is therefore not read as a gain in sensitivity.

Why effort would move the criterion rather than sensitivity can be framed by four accounts. A resource account, in which the grip competes with perception for limited capacity, predicts noisier evidence and a shallower function [@azer2023]. That was not observed here, as @sun2026handgrip also concluded. A second account treats the shift as caution: under a concurrent physical demand, observers may require more evidence before reporting a change. In the same cohort, high grip also improved metacognitive efficiency, an effect that appeared to be driven by lower confidence on errors at the easiest auditory offset [@sun2026handgrip]. A decision state that is both more conservative and better at registering its own errors fits caution better than degraded input, although the two grip effects did not covary across participants [@sun2026handgrip], so they may not share one mechanism. A third account is that arousal acts on bias directly. Pupil-linked phasic arousal has been associated with a reduction of choice bias [@deGee2020pupil], but here the task-evoked response did not predict the rate of "different" responses, so trial-wise phasic arousal did not carry the effort effect in this sample. A fourth account places the shift at the response rather than the decision. "Different" was always reported with the right index finger and "same" with the right middle finger, and a left-hand grip could bias right-hand responding toward one finger. Neither the psychometric analysis nor the diffusion model can separate a decision criterion from a bias in response mapping. A design that counterbalances the mapping could.

The pupil measures responded to effort less than expected. Pupil size during the grip did not differ significantly between grip levels, whereas Chapter 1 found that high effort enlarged the pupil in younger adults in every task [CONFIRM: Chapter 1 pupil result after the Chapter 1 time-axis check]. Several features of this sample could contribute. Older adults have smaller pupils and a reduced range for dilation [@winn1994; @piquado2010]. The grip window begins soon after the pupil's response to the onset of the grip gauge (@fig-pupil-timecourse), which may obscure a smaller effort effect. The effect of effort varied considerably across participants, and only `r v_int("m2_n_participants")` of the `r v_int("m1_n_participants")` participants contributed to that model. Without a younger group measured in the same way, these data cannot show that the weaker effect reflects age. The TEPR was smaller under high effort, but grip release, the release cue, and the button press fall inside its window, and releasing a strong grip differs from releasing a light one. The TEPR is also measured relative to the pre-probe pupil, and evoked responses tend to be smaller when baseline pupil size is larger [@gilzenrat2010]. The effort difference in the TEPR therefore cannot be attributed to processing of the probe.

On trials when the pupil before the probe was larger than the participant's mean, the psychometric slope was shallower. That direction fits adaptive gain theory, in which higher tonic arousal accompanies a less task-focused control state [@astonjones2005; @gilzenrat2010], and the finding that performance declines at large baseline pupil sizes [@murphy2011]. The evidence is weak. The interval reaches zero, and the pre-probe window follows the standard and so contains the early response to it. The association is a hypothesis for a study with a clean pre-stimulus baseline rather than a finding this chapter rests on. The TEPR, summarized as a mean or as an area, was associated with neither the slope nor the rate of "different" responses. In this sample, the pupil did not carry the effect of effort on the judgment.

Several features of the design limit these conclusions. Grip release, its visual cue, and the button press all fall inside the task-evoked window, and the pre-probe window contains the early response to the standard. The response mapping was not counterbalanced. With two effort levels, the data cannot describe a dose–response relation or test an inverted-U relation between arousal and performance. This chapter has no younger group, so no effect can be attributed to age. Data were collected in an MRI scanner, which constrains luminance, posture, and noise. Pupil data were missing or unusable for `r v_int("n_no_tepr")` of the `r v_int("m1_n_participants")` participants, and high-effort trials were slightly more likely to be usable, although every pupil model included effort. Pupil size was recorded in arbitrary units. The behavioral model had no lapse rate, which bears on the reading of the slope interaction.

For older adults, holding a physical effort appears to change how readily a change is reported rather than how well it is perceived. That distinction matters wherever older adults must notice a change while exerting themselves: a more conservative criterion predicts more missed changes when the evidence is weak, without implying that perception itself is impaired. A study that counterbalances the response mapping, uses more than two effort levels, measures a pre-stimulus baseline free of other stimuli, and models confidence alongside choice could separate the caution and response-mapping accounts and test whether tonic arousal predicts discrimination. In this chapter, physical effort shifted older adults' criterion toward "same", and pupil-linked arousal did not account for that shift.

## Random-effects reduction

```{r}
#| label: reduction-table
#| tbl-cap: "Random-effects steps for each model. A step is accepted when the fit is not singular and the optimizer returns no convergence message."

red <- read_export("tbl_reduction.csv")
stopifnot(nrow(red) > 0L)
step_lab <- c(
  "1_maximal" = "Maximal",
  "2_uncorrelated" = "Uncorrelated slopes",
  "3_drop_b1_state" = "Drop pre-probe slope",
  "3_drop_tepr_state" = "Drop task-evoked slope",
  "specified_intercept" = "Intercept only",
  "same_as_M4b_3_drop_tepr_state" = "As accepted for the task-evoked model",
  "D-S1_drop_x_c" = "Drop offset slope"
)
re_lab <- c(
  "(1 + catch + x_c + effort_c + task_c | subject)" = "Intercept and slopes for catch, offset, effort, and task",
  "(1 + effort_c | subject)" = "Intercept and a slope for effort",
  "(1 + effort_c + x_c | subject)" = "Intercept and slopes for effort and offset",
  "(1 + catch + x_c + b1_state | subject)" = "Intercept and correlated slopes for catch, offset, and pre-probe pupil",
  "(1 + catch + x_c + b1_state || subject)" = "Intercept and uncorrelated slopes for catch, offset, and pre-probe pupil",
  "(1 + catch + x_c || subject)" = "Intercept and uncorrelated slopes for catch and offset",
  "(1 + catch + x_c + tepr_state | subject)" = "Intercept and correlated slopes for catch, offset, and the task-evoked response",
  "(1 + catch + x_c + tepr_state || subject)" = "Intercept and uncorrelated slopes for catch, offset, and the task-evoked response",
  "(1 | subject)" = "Intercept only",
  "(1 + catch || subject)" = "Intercept and an uncorrelated slope for catch"
)
stopifnot(all(red$Step %in% names(step_lab)))
stopifnot(all(red[["Random effects"]] %in% names(re_lab)))
conv <- red$Convergence
conv_lab <- ifelse(
  is.na(conv) | conv %in% c("NULL", ""),
  "None",
  ifelse(
    grepl("isSingular", conv, fixed = TRUE),
    "Boundary",
    ifelse(grepl("failed to converge", conv, fixed = TRUE), "Did not converge", NA_character_)
  )
)
stopifnot(!anyNA(conv_lab))
yn <- function(x) ifelse(as.logical(x), "Yes", "No")
display <- data.frame(
  Model = red$Model,
  Step = unname(step_lab[red$Step]),
  "Random effects" = unname(re_lab[red[["Random effects"]]]),
  Singular = yn(red$Singular),
  Convergence = conv_lab,
  Accepted = yn(red$Accepted),
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  knitr::kable(
    display,
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    longtable = TRUE,
    align = c("p{0.42in}", "p{1.15in}", "p{2.05in}", "p{0.62in}", "p{1.05in}", "p{0.62in}")
  )
} else {
  knitr::kable(display)
}
```

## Area under the curve {#sec-s1}

S1 replaces the TEPR mean in M4b with the gap-respecting area. M4b's accepted random-effects structure did not converge for that outcome (maximum absolute gradient `r v_num("s1_max_abs_grad")` against lme4's default tolerance of 0.002). The ladder was continued from that structure by dropping the offset random slope. That step was accepted (`r v_int("s1_nobs")` trials). The offset-by-state term was `r v("s1_x_c_teprauc_state_est")` (SE `r v("s1_x_c_teprauc_state_se")`), 95% CI `r v("s1_x_c_teprauc_state_ci")`, *p* `r S1_slope$p_fmt`. The state term was `r v("s1_teprauc_state_est")`, *p* `r S1_state$p_fmt`, and the catch-by-state term was `r v("s1_catch_teprauc_state_est")`, *p* `r S1_catch$p_fmt`. The area version agrees with M4b in the sense that none of these intervals excludes zero. M4b itself was not changed.

## Behavior in the pupil subsample {#sec-s2}

S2 fits M1's formula to the `r v_int("s2_nobs")` trials from the `r v_int("s2_n_participants")` participants who contributed to the TEPR sample. The maximal model was singular, so it was not accepted. The point estimates were `r v("s2_effort_c_est")` for effort (*p* `r S2_effort$p_fmt`), `r v("s2_catch_effort_c_est")` for catch-by-effort (*p* `r S2_catch$p_fmt`), and `r v("s2_x_c_effort_c_est")` for offset-by-effort (*p* `r S2_slope$p_fmt`). They are reported only to show the direction in this subset. They are not a second accepted test.

## Optimizer check {#sec-allfit}

M1, M4a, and M4b were re-estimated with the optimizers that ship with lme4 (`r v("allfit_optimizers")`). No key-term estimate from a converged optimizer differed from the accepted bobyqa estimate by more than 0.01. The largest absolute key-term deviation in that set was `r v("allfit_max_abs_dev")`.

:::
